q1: SELECT DISTINCT VIEWER_ID AS ID FROM VIEWS GROUP BY VIEW_DATE, VIEWER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ID FROM( SELECT VIEWER_ID ID, COUNT(DISTINCT ARTICLE_ID) CNT FROM VIEWS GROUP BY 1, VIEW_DATE ) T WHERE CNT >1

counterexample: INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, 201, '2023-01-01'); INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (1, 101, 201, '2023-01-02'); INSERT INTO VIEWS (ARTICLE_ID, AUTHOR_ID, VIEWER_ID, VIEW_DATE) VALUES (2, 102, 202, '2023-01-01');
explanation: Q1 groups by VIEW_DATE, which means it treats each unique combination of VIEWER_ID and VIEW_DATE as a separate group. Q2, on the other hand, does not group by VIEW_DATE, leading to a different interpretation of the data and potentially different results.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have at least two distinct VIEWER_IDs, each viewing the same ARTICLE_ID on different days. The difference in results will be whether Q1 considers the viewers as distinct based on the same ARTICLE_ID across different days, while Q2 does not group by VIEW_DATE and thus might treat the viewers differently.
